sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: Routing decides where packets should go when they travel between networks. Learn how routers acquire routes, choose a route, translate addresses, provide gateway redundancy, and divide physical interfaces logically.
bullets: Administrative distance, prefix length, and metric
sections.callout: LEARN ROUTES → CHOOSE ROUTE → FORWARD TRAFFIC → TRANSLATE ADDRESSES → PROVIDE REDUNDANCY

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: When a router has multiple ways to reach a destination, identify how each route was learned, how the router selects the route, and what technology changes or protects the path.
bullets: Most specific destination match → Prefix length

sections.title: Static and Dynamic Routing

entries.title: Static Routing
paragraphs: A static route is manually configured by an administrator. It is predictable and useful when a network is small, a path rarely changes, or a particular path must always be used. It does not automatically adapt to topology changes.
entries.memoryHook: ADMINISTRATOR TELLS THE ROUTER THE PATH.
entries.recognitionCue: A route manually entered by an administrator is a static route.

entries.title: Dynamic Routing
paragraphs: Dynamic routing lets routers exchange routing information and learn paths automatically. It fits larger or changing environments because learned routes can adapt when the topology changes.
entries.recognitionCue: Routers exchanging and updating route information indicates dynamic routing.

sections.callout: Manual configuration → Static. Automatic learning → Dynamic.

entries.title: Border Gateway Protocol (BGP)
paragraphs: BGP exchanges routing information between autonomous systems and is strongly associated with Internet-scale routing. An autonomous system is a network or group of networks under common administration.
entries.recognitionCue: Routing between autonomous systems or across the Internet → BGP.

entries.title: Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP)
paragraphs: EIGRP is a dynamic routing protocol strongly associated with Cisco environments. It learns internal routes and selects paths using routing metrics.

entries.title: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
paragraphs: OSPF is a link-state dynamic routing protocol. OSPF routers learn the topology, calculate preferred paths, and use cost as their metric.
entries.recognitionCue: A link-state protocol using cost → OSPF.

sections.title: Route Selection
paragraphs: A router can know several routes toward one destination. Prefix length, administrative distance, and metric answer different selection questions.

entries.title: Prefix Length
paragraphs: Prefix length states how many address bits identify the network. When several routes match a destination, the router prefers the most specific match—the longest prefix match. If 192.168.0.0/16 and 192.168.10.0/24 both match 192.168.10.50, /24 wins.
entries.memoryHook: More matching network bits = more specific route.

entries.title: Administrative Distance
paragraphs: Administrative distance represents the router's trust in the source of routing information. A lower administrative distance is generally preferred when routes to the same destination come from different sources.
entries.memoryHook: Which route source do I trust?

entries.title: Metric
paragraphs: A metric is a value a routing protocol uses to choose among paths it learned. Depending on the protocol, it can reflect cost, bandwidth, delay, or other path information. OSPF uses cost.
entries.memoryHook: Which path does this protocol prefer?

sections.callout: Destination specificity → Prefix length. Route-source trust → Administrative distance. Path quality inside a protocol → Metric.

sections.title: Address Translation
paragraphs: Private IPv4 addresses are not normally routed directly across the public Internet. Address translation allows privately addressed systems to communicate with external networks.

entries.title: Network Address Translation (NAT)
paragraphs: NAT changes IP address information as traffic crosses between networks and is commonly used to translate private IPv4 addresses to public IPv4 addresses.

entries.title: Port Address Translation (PAT)
paragraphs: PAT distinguishes sessions with port numbers so multiple internal devices can share one public IPv4 address. For example, 192.168.10.20:51001 and 192.168.10.21:51002 can map through the same public address.
entries.memoryHook: Many devices → one address → different ports.
entries.recognitionCue: Many hosts share one public address using unique ports → PAT.

sections.callout: Address translation → NAT. Address plus port translation → PAT.

sections.title: FHRP and Virtual IP

entries.title: First Hop Redundancy Protocol (FHRP)
paragraphs: FHRP provides default-gateway redundancy. Multiple routers can participate so another router can take over gateway duties if the active router fails.

entries.title: Virtual IP (VIP)
paragraphs: A VIP is a logical address not permanently tied to one physical interface. Hosts use the shared VIP as their default gateway, so the active physical router can change without requiring client reconfiguration.

sections.callout: FHRP is the redundancy mechanism; VIP is the shared logical address.

sections.title: Subinterfaces
paragraphs: A subinterface is a logical interface created from a physical router interface. One physical port can therefore support multiple logical networks or VLANs, such as separate logical interfaces beneath GigabitEthernet0/0.
sections.callout: One physical interface → multiple logical interfaces.

sections.title: Recognition Cues
bullets: Most specific route → Prefix length/longest prefix match
Many systems share address through ports → PAT
Logical divisions of one physical interface → Subinterfaces

entries.title: Static vs. Dynamic
paragraphs: Manual route → Static. Automatically learned route → Dynamic.

entries.title: Administrative Distance vs. Metric
paragraphs: Which route source is trusted? → Administrative distance. Which path does a protocol prefer? → Metric.

entries.title: Prefix Length vs. Metric
paragraphs: Most specific destination match → Prefix length. Best path according to the routing protocol → Metric.

entries.title: NAT vs. PAT
paragraphs: Address translation → NAT. Multiple hosts sharing an address through ports → PAT.

entries.title: FHRP vs. VIP
paragraphs: Gateway redundancy mechanism → FHRP. Logical shared address → VIP.

entries.title: Physical Interface vs. Subinterface
paragraphs: Hardware interface → Physical interface. Logical division of a physical interface → Subinterface.

sections.title: Maestro Recognition Sheet
bullets: One physical interface, multiple logical interfaces → Subinterfaces
